data.description: Malaysia's auto sales in November could be sequentially stronger, driven by more aggressive year-end discounting and festive promotions, Affin Hwang IB analyst Afifah Ishak says in a note. Affin Hwang maintains a neutral rating on the Malaysian auto and auto-parts sector, pegging MBM Resources as its top pick, citing its resilient earnings profile, underpinned by its associate stake in national carmaker Perodua. data.title: Australian shares recover from June low as miners rally
data.description:
Australian shares clawed back from a 5-1/2-month low on Monday, led by a rebound in battered mining and gold stocks, although losses in banks and economic slowdown concerns kept a lid on gains.

The S&P/ASX 200 index rose 0.1% to 8,600.1 by 0042 GMT after falling as much as 0.8% earlier in the session to its lowest level since June 9. The benchmark had declined 1.6% on Friday.

Mining stocks climbed 1.3%, recovering after the sub-index hit an eight-month low on Friday and shed more than 15% over the previous seven sessions. Heavyweights BHP and Rio Tinto gained 2% and 0.4%, respectively.

Gold miners rose 1.4%, snapping an eight-session losing streak after bullion prices jumped more than 1%. Evolution Mining advanced 2.7%.

However, a 0.6% decline in financials limited the broader market's gains. The sector was on track for a fifth straight day of losses, with the country's big four banks down between 0.3% and 1.4%.

Last week's soft jobs data pointed to easing labour market tightness and largely ruled out chances of further interest-rate hikes while stoking concerns about a possible economic slowdown.

Swaps now imply a 92.6% chance that the Reserve Bank of Australia will hold the cash rate steady next month, with rate cuts largely expected only from mid-2027.

Attention now turns to the October inflation report, due on Wednesday, for further clues on the central bank's policy outlook.

Technology stocks slipped 0.1%, tracking losses in Wall Street peers following an AI-driven selloff. Sector heavyweights Xero and WiseTech Global fell 1% and 0.3%, respectively.

Energy stocks fell 0.7%, tracking a decline in oil prices, with sector leaders Woodside Energy down 1.4% and Santos losing 0.3%.

Across the Tasman Sea, New Zealand's benchmark S&P/NZX 50 index fell 1.1% to 13,948, the lowest in about two weeks.

data.title: Steady Start Eyes For China Stock Market
data.description:
BEIJING (dpa-AFX) - The China stock market has moved lower in two straight sessions, sliding more than 50 points or 1.4 percent along the way. The Shanghai Composite Index now sits just above the 3,530-point plateau although it may find traction on Monday.

The global forecast for the Asian markets suggests volatility after last week's heavy selling, with technology shares likely to see continued selling pressure. The European and U.S. markets were sharply lower and the oversold Asian bourses are expected to at least open in the red.

The SCI finished sharply lower on Monday following losses from the technology, semiconductor, industrial, retail and mineral sectors.

For the day, the index slumped 43.83 points or 1.23 percent to finish at 3,533.79 after trading between 3,500.83 and 3,538.27. The Shenzhen Composite Index stumbled 72.65 points or 3.64 percent to end at 1,924.90.

The lead from Wall Street is brutal as the major averages opened flat on Friday but quickly headed sharply lower, accelerating deeper into the red throughout the day to end at session lows.

The Dow plunged 949.73 points or 1.93 percent to finish at 48,147.33, while the NASDAQ plummeted 1,261.47 points or 5.28 percent to close at 22,617.73 and the S&P 500 tumbled 265.44 points or 3.70 percent to end at 6,910.39.

For the week, the NASDAQ nosedived by 10 percent, the S&P 500 plummeted by 8.6 percent and the Dow plunged by 8 percent.

The sell-off on Wall Street came amid continued weakness among technology stocks, as reflected by the steep drop by the tech-heavy NASDAQ. A steep drop by shares of Anthropic (ANT) weighed on the tech sector following its record-breaking initial public offering on Thursday.

Concerns about the outlook for interest rates also contributed to the selling pressure, with at least a quarter-point rate hike seen as a near-certainty at the Federal Reserve's monetary policy next month. Traders are increasingly worried the Fed will continue to raise rates in the coming months in order to combat stubborn inflation.

Crude oil prices moved higher on Friday as vessels transiting the Strait of Hormuz continue to suffer attacks. West Texas Intermediate crude for December delivery was up by $0.72 or 0.87 percent at $83.93 per barrel.

data.title: RHB Bank's Growth Strategy Could Support Earnings Despite Near-Term Headwinds — Market Talk
data.description: RHB Bank's near-term earnings may face headwinds from weaker treasury income and potential asset quality pressures amid rising inflation, Public Investment Bank analyst Wong Ling Ling says in a note. However, the bank is expected to manage these risks through resilient fundamentals and its three-year corporate strategy, which targets 12% return on equity by 2027, she says. Loan expansion, stronger current and savings account deposits, higher fee-based income and cost discipline are expected to support earnings growth, she adds. Wong believes RHB's strong fundamentals, attractive dividend yields of about 6% and undemanding valuations could support an attractive risk-reward proposition. Public IB initiates coverage on RHB Bank with an outperform rating and 8.60 ringgit target price. Shares are 0.1% lower at 7.64 ringgit. (yingxian.wong@wsj.com)

data.title: South Korean shares slump nearly 3% on AI-driven tech selloff despite policy pledge
data.description:
Key points:
  • Benchmark KOSPI index falls, foreigners net buyers
  • Korean won strengthens against dollar
  • South Korea benchmark bond yield flat

South Korean shares fell roughly 3% on Monday as a government pledge to deploy market stabilisation funds failed to ease concerns over the AI trade and a broader technology selloff.

The benchmark KOSPI was down 132.98 points, or 2.73%, at 4,736.98 by 0034 GMT, hovering at the lowest level since January.

On Sunday, authorities said they would deploy market stabilisation funds immediately if conditions worsened, after the South Korean benchmark index tumbled to a 10-month low last week.

Shares of chipmaker Samsung Electronics fell 3.44%, while peer SK Hynix lost 2.16%.

Among other index heavyweights, battery maker LG Energy Solution slid 1.00%, while Hyundai Motor and sister automaker Kia Corp were down 3.14% and 2.95%, respectively.

The muted response to Seoul's policy rollout suggested investors remain more concerned about the outlook for global technology stocks than local efforts to shore up sentiment.

The sharp selloff on Monday underscores how rapidly changes in Wall Street sentiment toward AI-related spending can ripple through Asia's technology supply chain.

Investors have increasingly questioned whether massive AI investments will generate returns quickly enough to justify the costs.

The market breadth remained negative, with 810 of the 896 traded issues declining against only 68 advancers.

The benchmark bond yield held flat in early trading as investors weighed domestic policy interventions against global equity headwinds.

data.title: South Korea, China, Taiwan regulators step in to rescue stock markets - Here are the steps they are taking
data.description:
Stock market regulators in China, Taiwan, and South Korea are stepping up to curb the fallout from the sell-off witnessed in Wall Street's AI trade, which has taken the Nasdaq 100 index into "bear market territory" and the Dow Jones and S&P 500 into a "technical correction".

Markets in all the three countries are steeply below the peaks they had surged to in the first half of the year, as the AI trade unwound, and concerns were raised over the financials of many companies.

Here are the steps regulators are taking to prevent any further fallout:

China

In China, the minimum margin requirement for investors buying securities with borrowed funds will fall to 80% from 100% on November 30, as per a notice issued by the Shanghai, Shenzhen, and Beijing stock exchanges, with approvals from the China Securities Regulatory Commission. The figure was raised to 100% in January to curb excess leverage risks.

According to the Xinhua news agency citing the regulator, the measure could unlock additional funds worth $60 billion.

The CSI 300 index has also slumped into a bear market after a 8% fall in October, marking its worst monthly performance in more than a decade, as economic weakness and a sharp fall in tech shares weighed.

Earlier this month, the People's Bank of China had said that it will conduct more than 100 billion yuan worth of swap operations to provide liquidity to securities firms, fund managers, and insurers, along with a relending program for share buybacks and stake increases, the interest rate for which was cut to 1% from 1.25% earlier.

South Korea

The poster boy of the Asia-Pacific AI trade also announced phased measures to calm the markets down amidst rising volatility.

Moves announced by the Korean authorities include ensuring a stock stabilization fund to be put in place to respond when needed. The move was announced by top financial officials on Sunday after an emergency meeting.

According to analysts, the government is preparing a 10 trillion won market stabilization fund, although the size looks insufficient to materially change the near-term sentiment.

Despite the measures, the KOSPI is down another 3% on Monday morning, while the Japanese stock markets are shut on account of a holiday.

"A sustained return to tech likely requires clearer resolution of Nvidia-related uncertainty, evidence that AI demand remains resilient despite tighter US chip export to China, and geopolitical easing that brings oil meaningfully lower," Shawn Oh of NH Investment & Securities said.

Taiwan

Over the weekend, Taiwan also announced a blanket ban on short-selling in stocks below their previous day's closing price. The Taiwanese TAIEX fell 18% last week, to mark its worst weekly fall since 1991.

The regulator also said that they have been buyers in stocks and urged investors to keep calm amidst the sell-off.

data.title: Australia's Victoria State Election Could Be a Watershed — Market Talk
data.description: Voters in Australia's southern state of Victoria are expected to hand the current Labor government a huge defeat at elections on Saturday. The mood is grim for the party, and if the drubbing is delivered, questions will be asked about what it means for the federal Labor government. It is likely to officially establish the right-wing populist One Nation party as a force that could impact the status quo in the federal arena. History has shown that voters can vote one way at state level and then another at federal elections. But Saturday's poll feels like it will be a watershed in Australian politics and the fallout could have big ramifications.(james.glynn@wsj.com; @JamesGlynnWSJ)

data.title: Two Chinese copper smelters blend concentrate overseas to boost supply, sources say
data.description:
Key points:
  • China Minmetals starts overseas blending on trial basis in third quarter, sources say
  • China Copper has engaged in overseas blending for around one year, sources say
  • CRU pegs global copper concentrate deficit at 289,000 metric tons this year

Two large Chinese smelters have begun blending copper concentrate at a Malaysian port in a bid to boost supply amid a worsening feedstock shortage, four people with knowledge of the matter told Reuters.

China is by far the world's largest copper ore processor. But its rules strictly limit the allowable levels of toxins such as arsenic, meaning that only about one-fifth of concentrate produced outside the country meets import standards.

Blending higher-standard concentrate grades with those containing more toxins can allow more concentrate volumes to meet Chinese regulations. China, however, limits the number of different concentrates that can be blended domestically.

So, in order to broaden the availability of supply that can be processed in China, integrated producer China Minmetals Nonferrous Metals and smelter China Copper have been blending complex copper concentrate containing high impurities in Port Klang, Malaysia, the people said.

China Copper has engaged in overseas blending for around a year, while China Minmetals started doing so on a trial basis in the third quarter of this year, two of the people said.

It was not immediately clear how much copper concentrate the two smelters have blended in the Malaysian port.

China Minmetals and China Copper did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

The blending of complex copper concentrates has been allowed in bonded zones at domestic ports since 2020 and currently takes place at ports including Dalian, Yantai and Fangcheng.

However, blending overseas provides flexibility to mix several different types of concentrate while more stringent requirements apply for blending domestically, said one of the people.

International trading houses have long blended concentrates at ports outside China to meet its import standards. The overseas blending by the two Chinese smelters, however, has not been previously reported.

All the people requested anonymity as the information is not public.

The copper concentrate shortage worsened this year as smelting capacity expanded and disruptions reduced mined supply, driving unexpectedly high production cuts in China in the fourth quarter.

Consultancy CRU pegged the global copper concentrate deficit at 289,000 metric tons this year, versus 2,000 tons in 2025. Analysts expect mined copper supply to improve in 2027, but not enough to fill the gap.

Global copper concentrate supply is projected to grow by 4% in 2027 following a 0.4% rise this year, according to CRU.
